source.title: The Dollar's World
source.summary: How the US dollar became the global reserve currency and what that means for Muslim-majority economies.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: From Bretton Woods to the Nixon shock to the petrodollar arrangement. The US dollar's journey to global reserve status. The dollar system provides real stability and liquidity that the world depends on. But it creates asymmetric vulnerability for peripheral economies: oil priced in dollars, debt denominated in dollars, vulnerability to Federal Reserve decisions made with American interests in mind. This episode traces how reserve currency status works in practice, what "exorbitant privilege" actually means, and how Muslim-majority economies navigate a system they didn't design but can't avoid.

thread: The petrodollar system means oil prices move with American monetary policy, not Middle Eastern production. When the Fed raises rates, oil-importing countries pay twice.
Bretton Woods made the dollar convertible to gold at $35 per ounce. Nixon ended that in 1971, but the dollar stayed global by becoming the oil currency.
Reserve currency status gives America "exorbitant privilege" — they can print money to pay foreign debts while others must earn dollars first.

linkedin.post: The petrodollar arrangement reveals how monetary policy travels across borders in ways most people never consider. When the Federal Reserve adjusts interest rates, they're making decisions with American economic interests in mind. But those decisions ripple through every oil transaction on earth. Oil-importing countries find themselves paying twice when the Fed tightens — once for more expensive oil, once for the stronger dollars needed to buy it. This is the hidden architecture of "exorbitant privilege." America can print money to pay foreign debts while peripheral economies must first earn those same dollars to participate in global trade. The journey from Bretton Woods to the Nixon shock to today's dollar system shows how reserve currency status works in practice. Muslim-majority economies navigate a system they didn't design but can't escape. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-mm-3

short_video.title: Why Oil Prices Follow the Fed
short_video.hook: Oil prices don't just respond to Middle Eastern production — they follow American monetary policy
short_video.voiceover: The petrodollar system creates a hidden connection between Federal Reserve decisions and global oil prices. When the Fed raises interest rates for American economic reasons, oil-importing countries pay twice. Once for more expensive oil, once for the stronger dollars needed to buy it. This is America's exorbitant privilege in action. They can print money to pay foreign debts while other economies must first earn those same dollars. The system traces back to the Nixon shock in 1971, when dollar-gold convertibility ended but dollar dominance continued through oil.
